MSK–SKIN · LECTURE COMPANION

Leg and Foot

Understand the compartments and move through the vascular, nerve, tendon and fascial pathways until the clinical findings become predictable.

Shannon Barwick, Ph.D. · November 17, 2026 · Lecture-based with labeled Step 1 enrichment

Learning Objectives

  1. Explain leg compartment organization, muscle actions, innervation, blood supply, crural fascia, and compartment syndrome.
  2. Identify major tibial, fibular, and foot landmarks, projections, and palpation points.
  3. Localize lesions of tibial, common fibular, superficial fibular, and deep fibular nerves from motor/sensory loss.
  4. Describe arterial supply, venous drainage, and the posterior tibial/dorsalis pedis pulse examinations.
  5. Differentiate superficial from deep veins and explain the significance of deep vein thrombosis.
  6. Describe the tarsal tunnel, its contents, and clinical significance.
  7. Describe plantar fascia, intrinsic muscles, major foot-supporting structures, nerves, and arteries.
  8. Explain tarsal tunnel syndrome, DVT, plantar fasciitis, tibial injury, and foot drop; localize sciatic branch lesions.
  9. Identify anterior/lateral leg and dorsal-foot structures on the course's radiographs, MRI, and CT.

Big Picture

Learn the geography first: tibia and fibula frame fascia-enclosed spaces; each compartment has a predictable nerve and action. Follow posterior tendons behind the medial malleolus into the sole; follow the anterior tibial artery onto the dorsal foot; then use sensory territories to localize injury.

Source priority: course lecture slides and attached 18-page lecture handout govern course content. Green-shaded First Aid boxes are selective Step 1 bridges, not additional claims about what the professor taught.

01 · Orientation, osteology & movements

Before learning lesions, know where the bones, fascia and tendons sit relative to each other.

Tibia: the medial weight-bearing leg bone. The tibial plateau articulates proximally; tibial tuberosity receives the patellar tendon; the posterior soleal line anchors soleus; the distal projection is the medial malleolus. The intercondylar eminence projects between plateaus.

Fibula: slender lateral bone; the head and neck are proximal, and the lateral malleolus is distal. The interosseous membrane spans tibia to fibula. The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck, explaining vulnerability at that landmark.

Foot skeleton: tarsals are calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid and medial/intermediate/lateral cuneiforms. The calcaneal tuberosity forms the heel; the sustentaculum tali supports the talus; the trochlea is the superior articular dome of talus. The course uses “Tiger Cubs Need MILC” for tarsal orientation.

MovementVisualizeMain compartment pattern
DorsiflexionToes toward skyAnterior leg / deep fibular nerve
PlantarflexionStand on toesPosterior leg / tibial nerve
InversionPlantar surface turns mediallyTibialis anterior and posterior
EversionPlantar surface turns laterallyLateral fibularis muscles; tertius assists
COMMON CONFUSION
A muscle can have two actions: tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts, whereas tibialis posterior plantarflexes and inverts. Eversion alone does not tell you whether fibularis tertius or the lateral fibularis muscles are functioning.

02 · The four functional leg compartments

Think of crural fascia as a nonexpandable sleeve and of the septa as walls creating constrained spaces.

CompartmentMusclesMain actionNerveMain arterial supply
AnteriorTA, EDL, EHL, fibularis tertiusDorsiflex; extend toesDeep fibularAnterior tibial
LateralFibularis longus, brevisEvertSuperficial fibularPerforators of fibular artery
Superficial posteriorGastrocnemius, plantaris, soleusPlantarflexTibialPosterior tibial system
Deep posteriorPopliteus, FDL, tibialis posterior, FHLToe flexion, inversion, plantarflexion; knee unlockTibialPosterior tibial and fibular

The crural fascia is continuous with fascia lata. The posterior intermuscular septum separates lateral from posterior compartments; the transverse intermuscular septum divides superficial and deep posterior compartments. When bleeding/swelling increases pressure inside this restrictive envelope, perfusion of muscles and nerves can be compromised.

MUST KNOW
Compartment syndrome is a limb-threatening consequence of increased pressure within a fascial compartment. Severe pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early clues; pulses may remain present. Urgent surgical evaluation is required.
FIRST AID CONNECTION
The board-relevant sequence is injury/hemorrhage → increased intracompartmental pressure → reduced microvascular perfusion → ischemic neuropathy and myonecrosis. A palpable distal pulse does not exclude early compartment syndrome.
Which compartment is impaired if a patient can plantarflex but cannot actively dorsiflex?

Anterior compartment (deep fibular nerve and anterior tibial supply).

Follow each tendon from its proximal attachment across the joint to predict motion.

Gastrocnemius versus soleus: gastrocnemius crosses the knee and ankle, so resistance with knee extended emphasizes it; soleus is tested with knee flexed ~90°. Both insert by calcaneal tendon and are supplied by the tibial nerve (lecture denotes L4–S3).

Popliteus: a deep posterior knee muscle that unlocks the extended knee by rotation. FDL flexes toes 2–5; FHL flexes hallux; tibialis posterior inverts and supports medial longitudinal arch. These three tendons continue behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel.

HIGH YIELD
Calcaneal (Achilles) reflex: tap tendon → stretch afferent/efferent reflex circuit → plantarflexion; the lecture specifies S1 and S2 nerve roots.
CLINICAL CONNECTION
Calcaneal tendon rupture may follow forceful dorsiflexion under eccentric plantarflexor load, with a “pop,” posterior ankle pain and weakened plantarflexion (lecture slide 24).
Why is flexing the knee a useful way to test soleus more selectively?

Gastrocnemius crosses the knee and is relatively shortened when the knee is flexed; soleus crosses only the ankle.

04 · Arteries, superficial veins & DVT

Trace vessels from popliteal artery into the leg and from the dorsal venous arch toward proximal veins.

Popliteal artery divides into anterior and posterior tibial pathways. The anterior tibial artery traverses the interosseous membrane into the anterior leg and continues onto the dorsum as dorsalis pedis. The posterior tibial artery passes through the soleal arch and tarsal tunnel, then branches into medial and lateral plantar arteries. The fibular (peroneal) artery supplies deep/lateral leg regions through perforators.

PulseWhere to place fingertipsWhy
Posterior tibialPosterior to medial malleolus, within tarsal-tunnel region with foot relaxedAssess distal perfusion; compare sides
Dorsalis pedisDorsum of foot just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendonContinuation of anterior tibial; compare sides
Superficial systemCourse / drainageDeep system
Great saphenousAnterior to medial malleolus → medial leg/thigh → femoral veinFemoral vein
Small saphenousPosterior to lateral malleolus → posterior leg → popliteal veinPopliteal vein
Dorsal venous archFeeds great/small saphenous pathwaysPosterior tibial and other deep veins accompany arteries

Deep vein thrombosis: immobility, surgery, bed rest or restrictive casts/bandages slow deep venous blood flow. The lecturer highlights venous stasis and possible warmth, swelling, and erythema. A thrombus can embolize to pulmonary arteries, making new dyspnea a warning sign.

FIRST AID CONNECTION
Virchow triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability) organizes the lecture’s immobility and postsurgical risk factors. DVT can be clinically silent; unilateral findings alone cannot confirm or exclude it.
A postoperative patient has new unilateral leg swelling followed by shortness of breath. What links these findings?

Deep venous thrombus may embolize to pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary embolism).

05 · Peripheral nerve maps and lesion localization

Name the affected nerve by combining movement weakness with the exact sensory territory.

Injury siteMotor loss to predictSensory pattern / distinguishing clue
Sciatic nerve (proximal)Multiple posterior-leg and fibular-compartment deficits; may affect hamstringsMixed tibial + fibular distributions; broader than isolated foot drop
Common fibular at fibular neckDorsiflexion and eversion weakened → foot dropMuch of dorsum of foot and anterolateral leg affected; plantar surface often spared
Deep fibularDorsiflexion and toe extension weak; if distal lesion, EDB/EHB weaknessFirst dorsal web space
Superficial fibularEversion weak; dorsiflexion largely preservedMost dorsum of foot except first web space; lateral leg
Tibial nervePlantarflexion, toe flexion, inversion impaired according to lesion levelPlantar foot sensory loss; tendon reflex may be reduced with high lesion
Tibial in tarsal tunnelIntrinsic plantar weakness/symptoms; extrinsic posterior muscles sparedPlantar/medial heel symptoms; tarsal-tunnel entrapment

Peripheral nerve versus dermatome: a dermatome maps one spinal nerve root; a named peripheral cutaneous nerve carries fibers from several roots and supplies a different territory. Separate L5 root disease from common fibular nerve disease using the full motor pattern and associated findings rather than foot drop alone.

EXAM TRAP
An isolated superficial fibular lesion produces eversion weakness without classic foot drop; isolated deep fibular lesion produces dorsiflexion weakness with characteristic first web-space sensory deficit. Common fibular injury combines both.
LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE
Fibular neck injury → common fibular nerve → loss of anterior and lateral leg function → steppage gait/foot drop; compare with isolated L5 radiculopathy, which can also weaken inversion (tibialis posterior via tibial nerve).
What is the best single sensory site to test for deep fibular nerve function?

Skin between the hallux and second toe—the first dorsal web space.

The patient cannot evert but dorsiflexes normally. Which branch is most likely affected?

Superficial fibular nerve, which supplies fibularis longus and brevis.

06 · Tarsal tunnel and its clinical correlations

This tunnel is the medial ankle’s neurovascular passage beneath a strong retaining band.

Boundary: posterior to medial malleolus, deep to flexor retinaculum. Anterior → posterior order: tibialis posterior tendon → flexor digitorum longus tendon → posterior tibial artery → tibial nerve → flexor hallucis longus tendon. The lecturer’s mnemonic is Tom, Dick, And Nervous Harry.

Mechanism: swollen synovial tendon sheaths or other volume increase within the confined tunnel compress the tibial nerve. The lecture describes pain between medial malleolus and heel that worsens with movement. Since tibial nerve reaches plantar foot from this point, tingling/numbness or weakness in plantar nerve territories can help localize a lesion distal to the posterior calf.

COMMON CONFUSION
Tarsal tunnel = tibial nerve beneath flexor retinaculum (medial ankle); carpal tunnel = median nerve beneath flexor retinaculum (wrist). Their similarity is structural, not innervation.
Which artery is located next to the tibial nerve in the tunnel?

Posterior tibial artery (anterior to tibial nerve in the slide’s listed order).

07 · Fascia, intrinsic muscles and arches of the foot

Layer the plantar foot from superficial to deep, then add the neurovascular tree.

The plantar aponeurosis invests plantar musculature and contributes to arch integrity. Strain produces plantar heel/medial foot pain; the lecture emphasizes that pain may ease as the day progresses in early plantar fasciitis.

1Flexor digitorum brevisFlexes toes 2–5Medial plantar
1Abductor digiti minimiAbducts/flexes toe 5Lateral plantar
2Quadratus plantaeAssists FDL; corrects oblique FDL pullLateral plantar
2Lumbricals (4)MTP flexion + IP extension toes 2–5Medial plantar to 1st; lateral plantar to 2nd–4th
3Flexor digiti minimi brevisFlexes proximal phalanx toe 5Superficial lateral plantar
3Adductor hallucis (oblique/transverse)Hallux adduction; transverse archDeep lateral plantar
3Flexor hallucis brevisFlexes proximal hallux phalanxMedial plantar
4Plantar interossei (3)PAD: adduct toes 3–5; MTP flexionLateral plantar
4Dorsal interossei (4)DAB: abduct toes 2–4; MTP flexionLateral plantar
DorsumExtensor hallucis brevisExtend halluxDeep fibular
DorsumExtensor digitorum brevisExtends toes 2–4 alongside EDLDeep fibular

Medial plantar nerve supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and first lumbrical. Lateral plantar nerve supplies most other plantar intrinsics, including quadratus plantae, abductor digiti minimi, adductor hallucis, interossei and lateral three lumbricals. The deep fibular nerve supplies EDB/EHB on the dorsum.

HIGH YIELD
Plantar interossei (3) = PAD (adduct digits 3–5); dorsal interossei (4) = DAB (abduct digits 2–4). Both receive lateral plantar nerve.
MSK CONNECTION
Tibialis posterior, FDL, FHL and plantar aponeurosis reinforce longitudinal arches. The course’s muscle-function map helps explain why tendon dysfunction changes foot support.
The first lumbrical is spared but the lateral three are paralyzed. Which plantar nerve branch is most likely affected?

Lateral plantar nerve.

Why does quadratus plantae assist toe flexion instead of simply duplicating FDL?

It adjusts the oblique vector of FDL pull, making flexion of lateral four toes more aligned.

08 · Image recognition and practical localization

Recognize bone position, fascial regions, vessels and tendons in the specific teaching views.

Visual sequence on an axial slice: identify tibia (large medial), fibula (smaller lateral), interosseous membrane, anterior extensors, lateral fibularis group, posterior superficial calf bulk, then the deep flexors. For X-ray, trace the tibia/fibula to malleoli and then identify tarsals before metatarsals.

PRACTICAL IMAGE
Practice pointing to a region without labels, naming its muscle group, characteristic action, nerve supply, and nearest major artery. These linked answers are more useful than memorizing cross-section colors alone.
On an axial calf section, which compartment is directly behind the tibia/fibula but deep to the soleus?

Deep posterior compartment.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

The concepts that allow you to reason through nearly every lesion vignette in this lecture.

Four-compartment map

Nerve + movement + location identify which functional compartment failed.

The fibular neck

A proximal common fibular lesion simultaneously weakens dorsiflexion and eversion.

Tibial tendon course

Posterior muscles feed the tarsal tunnel, which links tendon mechanics to plantar nerve and artery distribution.

Posterior versus anterior blood flow

Posterior tibial becomes plantar branches; anterior tibial becomes dorsalis pedis.

Plantar layers

Most intrinsic muscles are lateral plantar; the specific medial plantar exceptions are testable.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

A small set of lecture-adjacent Step 1 bridges, intentionally separate from tested course facts.

  1. Fascial pressure → ischemia: early compartment syndrome may still have distal pulses.
  2. Common fibular lesion at neck → foot drop: anterior/lateral compartment weakness, broad dorsal sensory loss.
  3. DVT → pulmonary embolism: Virchow triad contextualizes immobility after surgery.
  4. Peripheral neuropathy versus radiculopathy: compare tibialis posterior inversion with common fibular distribution in foot-drop localization.
  5. Medial ankle tibial compression → plantar symptoms: distinguish tarsal tunnel from a proximal tibial lesion.
